newsitem.title: UK: London's transport network starved of capital - LT.
newsitem.headline: London's transport network starved of capital - LT.

text.p: London's public transport network is being deprived of investment and things could get worse, industry chiefs said on Wednesday.

London Transport told Britain's parliamentary Transport Select Committee -- a body of politicians briefed to monitor the transport network -- that funding for the next three years is about 700 million pounds less than it had expected.

As a result of that and a long-term shortfall in investment, "the service on the (underground train) system may become less reliable," David Bailey, director of development at London Underground Ltd, said.
London Transport controls both the underground train service, known as the tube, and acts as an umbrella organisation over privatised bus services in Britain's capital.
The 700 million shortfall is partly due to cuts in core funding and partly due to a cost overrun of an extension to one of the underground lines.
Bailey catalogued a long list of tube stations where refurbishment and renewal plans have had to be delayed because of a lack of capital.
LT's deposition to the committee said there remains a long-term investment backlog of 1.2 billion pounds.

"Stop/go capital, which we have tended to get, is very wasteful and very difficult to work with," London Transport's chairman Peter Ford told the collection of MPs. "And the backlog in investment is likely to rise again up to the millennium."
LT estimates it needs about 350 million pounds in investment each year to keep the system on an even keel. To implement key improvements would take much more.

But after funding cuts in Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke's November budget, even that amount will not be available. LT forecast the backlog in investment would have increased by a further 300 million pounds by 2002/03.

One of the major burdens was the increased costs for the Jubilee Line Extension -- a new underground artery that will link the centre of the capital to the office developments to the east of the city, such as Canary Wharf.
Part of the cost increase was caused by the collapse of tube tunnels elsewhere in the network, which held up engineering works. The government will cover that.

But the rest of the overshoot will come out of London Underground budgets. "It was always going to be incredibly difficult to estimate the total cost," Ford said. "It's an incredibly complex project."

Investment levels are so anaemic that even safety may become an issue. Derek Tunnicliffe, London Underground's managing director, told the committee that the tube system was subject to the best safety legislation in the UK and stressed that safety was the first priority.
"But we are less content now than perhaps we have been," he said. With the 10th anniversary of a fire at Kings Cross station which claimed 30 lives only months away, those words resonate powerfully.
Ford said London's public transport network was a key issue for tourists and investors alike. "It affects people's whole perception of London."

And he dismissed the idea that the private finance initiative -- a government scheme to entice private investment into infrastructure projects -- was a substitute for core investment. It can only be a supplement, he said.
